ref: Propugnaculum fidei (Venetiis 1608), Prefatio Authoris, p. 2 (signature/page of the 'Prefatio'); PDF p. 48 of archive.org item bub_gb_lMhEuhL-bVEC (page image read)
quote_orig: In hoc igitur tertio statu, scilicet: post tempora Beati Gregorij tempore Heraclij surrexit contra Ecclesiam Dei, & contra veritatem quidam draco diabolicus, homo lubricus, & obscenis actibus deditus nomine Mahumetus, qui consilio illius, & auxilio qui mendax est, & pater eius, legem mendacissimam, & nephariam composuit, quasi ex ore Dei; quam legem appellavit Alchoranum, quasi collectarium praeceptorum Dei. Hic Mahumetus super alios, qui unquam fuerunt, persecutus est Ecclesiam Dei.
own_translation_en: In this third state, that is, after the time of blessed Gregory, in the time of Heraclius, a certain diabolical dragon, a slippery man given over to obscene deeds, named Mahumetus, rose against the Church of God and against the truth. By the counsel and help of him who is a liar and his father, he composed a most lying and nefarious law, which he called Alchoranum, as if it came from the mouth of God, a collection of God's precepts. This Mahumetus persecuted the Church of God more than all who have ever existed.
licence_note: Public Domain Mark 1.0 per archive.org metadata; 1608 print. The English is the team's own literal translation (no PD English exists). The phrase 'homo lubricus' read as 'homo lu-' / 'bricus' line break in the page image (joined).
keys: draco diabolicus, homo lubricus
legem mendacissimam, & nephariam composuit
Hic Mahumetus super alios, qui unquam fuerunt, persecutus est Ecclesiam Dei
what_it_says: Riccoldo says Muhammad was a diabolical, lustful man who, with the counsel of the devil, composed a lying law that he falsely presented as coming from God. He claims Muhammad persecuted the Church more than anyone before him.
context: This is the opening of Riccoldo's preface, where he describes the 'third state' of the Church's corruption after Gregory the Great, placing Muhammad in the reign of Heraclius. It sets the tone for the whole treatise, which he wrote after years of studying the Qur'an in Arabic in Baghdad.
limits: Latin is the 1608 Serafini print, not the 15th-century Picenus back-translation (1543/1550), which reads differently ('homo quidam diabolicus, primogenitus Satanae, in libidinem proclivis'). Obscenis actibus / lubricus are invective, not a neutral description of Muhammad's life. Quoting a Dominican polemicist, so the team should present it as his own invective.

ref: Propugnaculum fidei (Venetiis 1608), Caput X (Decimum capitulum), p. 37 (signature 'C 3'); PDF p. 83 of archive.org item bub_gb_lMhEuhL-bVEC (page image read, crop at 250 dpi)
quote_orig: Hic Mahumetus fuit Antichristi praecursor, qui filio perditionis viam praeparavit in mundo; quae via & modus, quantum sit irrationabilis, patuit superius in 8. capitulo. Nam sicut dicit Augustinus, caetera potest homo (etiam nolens) credere autem non potest nisi volens.
own_translation_en: Here Mahumetus was the forerunner of the Antichrist, who prepared the way for the son of perdition in the world. The way and the method, insofar as it is irrational, was shown above in the eighth chapter. For, as Augustine says, a man can believe other things even unwillingly, but he cannot believe unless he is willing.
licence_note: Public Domain Mark 1.0 per archive.org metadata (1608 print). English is the team's own translation.
keys: Hic Mahumetus fuit Antichristi praecursor
qui filio perditionis viam praeparavit in mundo
caetera potest homo (etiam nolens) credere
what_it_says: Riccoldo classes Muhammad as the forerunner of Antichrist, who prepared the way of the 'son of perdition', and says the irrationality of his way was shown earlier in the eighth chapter.
context: This sentence closes Riccoldo's tenth chapter, on the violence of the Qur'an and of its law. He moves from the sword to Muhammad's place in eschatology, then argues that faith is a matter of the will, so a religion imposed by force cannot produce true belief.
limits: The Augustine attribution ('caetera potest homo ... credere autem non potest nisi volens') is Riccoldo's own citation and was NOT checked against Augustine's text in this session. The Antichrist classing is a standard medieval claim, not Riccoldo's private invention, but I did not verify its source in the literature. The preceding text of the chapter (not quoted) contains killing commands, which are excluded (see excluded.json).

ref: Propugnaculum fidei (Venetiis 1608), Caput III (Tertium capitulum: 'lex Saracenorum non est lex Dei'), p. 10 (signature 'Ertio/Tertio sciendum'); PDF p. 56 of archive.org item bub_gb_lMhEuhL-bVEC (page image read, crop at 250 dpi)
quote_orig: Tertio sciendum est, quod Alchoranus non est lex Dei, non enim attestatur ei nec vetus testamentum, nec Euangelium quae ambo Alchoranus testatur quod sint, verae lex Dei, sed ipse Mahumetus seipsum commendat, ipse de seipso testimonium perhibet. Nos autem invenimus legem Dei esse quandam cathenam continuam, ab eodem artifice fabricatam, ut unus anulus alteri cohereat, & correspondeat, & unus propheta de alio prophetat, & mentionem facit, & omnes alij prophetauerunt de Christo.
own_translation_en: Third, one must know that the Alchoranus is not the law of God, for neither the Old nor the New Testament bears witness to it, while both of them, which the Alchoranus itself testifies are the true law of God, Mahumetus commends himself, and he bears witness about himself. We, however, find that the law of God is a continuous chain, forged by one and the same craftsman, so that each link clings to the next and corresponds to it, and one prophet prophesies of another, and all the other prophets prophesied about Christ.
licence_note: Public Domain Mark 1.0 per archive.org metadata (1608 print). English is the team's own translation. The 1608 text has 'quod sint, verae lex Dei' (agreement as printed).
keys: non est lex Dei, non enim attestatur ei nec vetus testamentum
ipse Mahumetus seipsum commendat
omnes alij prophetauerunt de Christo
what_it_says: Riccoldo argues the Qur'an is not God's law because neither the Old nor the New Testament testifies to it, and because Muhammad alone bears witness to himself, unlike the chain of prophets who all point to Christ.
context: This opens the third chapter of the treatise (the table of contents lists it as the third principal error: 'quod lex haec non est lex Dei'). It is Riccoldo's Scripture argument, which sets the Qur'an against the Bible as a self-authenticating text.
limits: Latin is the 1608 print; the 1550 Picenus back-translation has similar sense but different wording. The 'quod sint, verae lex Dei' phrase is printed with a grammatical mismatch which I reproduced as printed. Riccoldo's argument assumes the Qur'an's own claim that the Gospel and Torah are God's law, which he takes as given.

famous.where_cited: Ferrero Hernandez 2021 (n.17) quotes this chapter-1 wording ('Primo igitur oportet scire...', 'Ipse namque Machometus cum Sabellio negat Trinitatem') and traces it to Peter the Venerable's Summa totius haeresis Saracenorum, citing Merigoux 1986 and Kritzeck 1964 (only the 2021 article was opened).

ref: Propugnaculum fidei (Venetiis 1608), Caput I (Primum capitulum: 'principales errores legis Saracenorum'), p. 5 (signature 'A 3'); PDF p. 51 of archive.org item bub_gb_lMhEuhL-bVEC (page image read, crop at 250 dpi for the first lines; the tail of the quote read on the 170-dpi page image)
quote_orig: Primo igitur oportet scire qui sunt principales errores, quos lex Saracenorum ponit, in quibus maxime legi Dei contrariatur. Et sciendum quod omnium antiquorum haereticorum feces quas diabolus in alios sparsim seminauerat, simul in Mahumetum reuomuit. Ipse namque Mahumetus cum Sabellio negat Trinitatem; ponit enim in Diuinis quendam binarium qui est numerus infamis, & alterius principium, ponit enim ipsam diuinam essentiam, & eius animam quasi alteram, & diuersam, unde Deum pluraliter loquentem introducit in Alchorano, & sic videtur ipsa, & ipse Christus essentiae a Deo, & Deo minor, & ei subditus, & in hoc conuenit cum Arrio, & Eunomio, qui ponebant Christum puram creaturam licet excellentissimam.
own_translation_en: First, one must know what are the principal errors that the law of the Saracens holds, by which it chiefly opposes the divine law. And one must know that the dregs of all the ancient heretics, which the devil had scattered here and there among others, he vomited up again into Mahumetus. For Mahumetus, with Sabellius, denies the Trinity; he posits in the divine a certain binary, which is an infamous number and the principle of otherness; he posits the divine essence itself and its soul as another and different, whence he introduces God speaking in the plural in the Alchoranus; and so it appears that Christ is of a different essence from God, less than God and subject to him. In this he agrees with Arius and Eunomius, who held that Christ was a pure creature, though most excellent.
licence_note: Public Domain Mark 1.0 per archive.org metadata (1608 print). English is the team's own translation. The phrase 'Ipse namque Mahumetus' is printed with 'Mahumetus' in 1608; the Mérigoux text quoted by Ferrero 2021 reads 'Machometus'.
keys: Ipse namque Mahumetus cum Sabellio negat Trinitatem
omnium antiquorum haereticorum feces
unde Deum pluraliter loquentem introducit in Alchorano
what_it_says: Riccoldo says Muhammad gathered and vomited up all the ancient heresies, and that he denies the Trinity like Sabellius. He says the Qur'an makes Christ a creature subordinate to God, as Arius and Eunomius did.
context: This is the opening of the first chapter, which lists the principal errors of the Qur'an. Riccoldo presents Islam as the summary of earlier heresies, which he treats as a Christian heresiological category.
limits: The 1608 print is not the critical text: Ferrero Hernandez 2021 quotes Merigoux's edition as 'Machometum' and 'ponit tamen in diuinis quendam binarium', where the 1608 print reads 'Mahumetus' and 'ponit enim in Diuinis quendam binarium'. The team must not present quote_orig as the Merigoux text. The sentence about the 'feces of the ancient heretics' is not Riccoldo's own coinage: Ferrero Hernandez 2021 (n.17) traces it to Peter the Venerable's Summa totius haeresis Saracenorum, which she cites via Kritzeck 1964 (not opened here). So the attribution to Riccoldo is his own adaptation of Peter. The passage is a doctrinal polemic, not a call to arms. Trinity arguments such as 'binarium' are the Latin polemicist's reading of the Qur'an; no check against the Arabic was done.
stance: own view (adapting Peter the Venerable, per Ferrero 2021)

ref: Propugnaculum fidei (Venetiis 1608), Caput VI (Sextum capitulum: 'lex Saracenorum contradicit sibi ipsi'), p. 18 (signature 'C 1'); PDF p. 64 of archive.org item bub_gb_lMhEuhL-bVEC (page image read, crops at 250 dpi)
quote_orig: Constat autem quod multae contrarietates in eo, & contradictiones inveniuntur. Nam ipse in pluribus locis dicit; quod Deus non dirigit errantem, & tamen ipse docet errare, ut dirigantur, & educantur de tenebris ad lucem, & de inuio ad directionem. Ipse etiam dixit se fuisse orphanum, & errantem. Constat enim quod fuit idolatra, & tamen dicit quod Deus fecit talem prophetam.
own_translation_en: Now it is established that many contrarieties and contradictions are found in it. For in many places he says that God does not guide the one who errs, and yet he himself teaches to err, so that they may be guided and led out of darkness into the light, and from the wayless into the way. He also said that he himself was an orphan and erring. For it is established that he was an idolater, and yet he says that God made him such a prophet.
licence_note: Public Domain Mark 1.0 per archive.org metadata (1608 print). English is the team's own translation. 'orphanum' is printed (not 'erroneum' as an earlier OCR reading suggested).
keys: Constat autem quod multae contrarietates in eo, & contradictiones inveniuntur
quod Deus non dirigit errantem
Ipse etiam dixit se fuisse orphanum, & errantem
what_it_says: Riccoldo argues the Qur'an contradicts itself: it says God does not guide the erring, yet it teaches error; Muhammad is said to have been an orphan who erred and an idolater, yet God made him a prophet.
context: This is the sixth chapter, in which Riccoldo argues the Qur'an is not God's law because it is internally inconsistent. The argument moves from the Qur'an's own claims about Muhammad to its teaching on guidance.
limits: The passage refers to the Qur'an's own verses as Riccoldo reads them (he cites the Qur'anic chapters he calls 'Elnasa' (women) and 'Elbacha(ra)' (cow)). He does not give Arabic. The chapter also reports killing commands, which are NOT quoted here (see excluded.json). 'Idolatra' is a polemical reading of Muhammad's pre-Islamic past.

ref: Propugnaculum fidei (Venetiis 1608), Caput I (Primum capitulum), p. 7 (signature 'A 4'); PDF p. 53 of archive.org item bub_gb_lMhEuhL-bVEC (page image read at 170 dpi)
quote_orig: Ipse tamen multum commendat psalterium, & alios prophetas, & Iob, & legem Moysi, sed super omnia alia commendat Euangelium Christi, & dicit quod Christus de ipso prophetavit in Euangelio dicens: Annuncio vobis denuncio Dei qui post me veniet, & nomen eius Mahumetus: hoc autem nomen asseruit esse scriptum ab aeterno in throno Dei in superiori parte ad dexteram. Ad haec autem omnia credenda, non ostendit miraculum, sed nudavit ensem, & ait se missum fuisse a Deo non in virtute miraculorum, sed in virtute armorum, haec autem quae praedicta sunt, sunt tantum principales errores, qui continentur in Alchorano, qui est lex Saracenorum, falsitates autem quae ibi continentur, sunt quasi infinitae.
own_translation_en: He himself greatly commends the Psalter, the other prophets, Job and the law of Moses, but above all he commends the Gospel of Christ, and says that Christ prophesied of him in the Gospel, saying: 'I announce to you, I proclaim, the one of God who will come after me, and whose name is Mahumetus,' and he asserts that this name was written from eternity in the throne of God on the right side above. For all these things to be believed, he showed no miracle, but drew his sword, and said that he had been sent by God not in the power of miracles but in the power of arms. These things which have been said are only the principal errors contained in the Alchoranus, which is the law of the Saracens; the falsehoods contained in it are almost infinite.
licence_note: Public Domain Mark 1.0 per archive.org metadata (1608 print). English is the team's own translation. The sentence quotes a Qur'anic claim (61:6) as Riccoldo renders it in Latin.
keys: non ostendit miraculum, sed nudavit ensem
non in virtute miraculorum, sed in virtute armorum
Annuncio vobis denuncio Dei qui post me veniet
what_it_says: Riccoldo says Muhammad's claim to be sent by God rested not on miracles but on the power of arms, and that he 'drew his sword' rather than showing a miracle. He says the Qur'an falsely claims Christ prophesied Muhammad.
context: This passage closes the first chapter's list of principal errors and explains how Riccoldo reads the Qur'an's claim to be the final revelation. He links the lack of miracles to the use of the sword, which is the core of his later argument on violence.
limits: Riccoldo describes the sword as a sign of coercion; the drawing of the sword is his interpretation of the Qur'an's claim, not a call to violence. The verses that Riccoldo reads as commands to kill are excluded in excluded.json. The Latin 'Annuncio vobis denuncio Dei' is a rendering of the Qur'anic claim about the messenger 'after me', not a Gospel text.
stance: own view (reporting the Qur'an's claims as Riccoldo reads them)

ref: Liber peregrinationis, cap. XXXIII ('Quod lex Sarracenorum est mendacissima', begins book p. 136), book p. 137; Laurent, Peregrinatores medii aevi quatuor (1864); PDF p. 148 of archive.org item peregrinatoresm00odorgoog (page image read at 120 dpi)
url: https://archive.org/details/peregrinatoresm00odorgoog (page image PDF p. 148 = book p. 137; text layer absent, djvu text https://archive.org/download/peregrinatoresm00odorgoog/peregrinatoresm00odorgoog_djvu.txt used to find the page)
quote_orig: Sed de alcorano loquamur, de quo iam non sunt contenti Sarraceni dicere, quod sit liber Machometi, sed vere sermo dei. Sed quomodo non fuit verecundatus ille deus, qui dixit alcoranum, quod tot mendacia manifeste ibi dixit? Nam ibi scriptum est in pluribus locis, quod Maria, mater Ihesu Christi, fuit filia Amram, patris Moysi et Aaron, quod fuit soror Moysi et Aaron, cum constet, quod Maria peperit Christum tempore Cesaris Augusti, qui regnabat Rome et iam habebat monarchiam.
own_translation_en: But let us speak of the Alcoran, of which the Saracens no longer are content to say that it is the book of Machometus, but truly the word of God. But how was that God not ashamed, who said the Alcoran, since he said so many manifest lies in it? For it is written in many places there that Mary, mother of Jesus Christ, was the daughter of Amram, father of Moses and Aaron, and that she was the sister of Moses and Aaron, although it is established that Mary bore Christ in the time of Caesar Augustus, who reigned at Rome and already held the monarchy.
licence_note: Pre-1900 publication; archive.org item shows no rights field (UNVERIFIED licence statement). English is the team's own literal translation (no PD English translation of this text exists that I found). Quote made from page image, word-level read at 120 dpi.
keys: Sed quomodo non fuit verecundatus ille deus, qui dixit alcoranum
quod tot mendacia manifeste ibi dixit
quod Maria, mater Ihesu Christi, fuit filia Amram, patris Moysi et Aaron
what_it_says: Riccoldo argues the Qur'an contains manifest falsehoods, notably that Mary the mother of Jesus is the sister of Moses and Aaron. He claims this is contradicted by the known historical date of Christ's birth under Augustus.
context: This is in the travel narrative, in chapter XXXIII ('the law of the Saracens is most lying'), which Riccoldo wrote during his years in the East. It is one of the arguments that the Qur'an mistakes the biblical chronology.
limits: The Latin is from Laurent's 1864 edition of the Itinerarium (from a 1351 copy). The claim about 'Miriam/Maria sister of Moses' is Riccoldo's reading of the Qur'anic 'sister of Aaron' expression; the team should not present it as an exact rendering of the Arabic. The 'twelve thousand lies' anecdote on the same page is a legend Riccoldo reports, not a verified statement of Muhammad.

ref: Propugnaculum fidei (Venetiis 1608), Prefatio Authoris, p. 3 (signature 'A 2' / 'PRO-' catchword); PDF p. 49 of archive.org item bub_gb_lMhEuhL-bVEC (page image read at 170 dpi)
quote_orig: Unde cum transissem maria, & deserta, & peruenissem ad famosissimam ciuitatem saracenorum Valdacum, ubi generale ipsorum, & solemne habetur studium, ibi pariter linguam, & litteram Arrabicam didici, et legem eorum diligentissime relegens, & studiose in scholis, & cum magistris ipsorum frequenter conferens; magis ac magis per experientiam apprehendi perversitatem praedictae legis, & cum incepissem in latinum transferre, tot inveni fabulas, falsitates, & blasphemias, et eadem per omnia in locis creberrimis repetita quod tunc attediatus dimisi. Et in attritione de praedictis blasphemijs scripsi quasdam epistolas ad Ecclesiam triumphantem per modum querelae amaricati animi. Nunc autem est mea intentio de summa veritate confisus confutare principales obscoenitates tam perfidiae legis.
own_translation_en: Then, when I had crossed many seas and deserts and had come to the famous city of the Saracens, Valdacum (Baghdad), where their general and solemn school of learning is held, there I learned the Arabic language and letters, and read their law most diligently, and studied it in their schools, often conferring with their teachers. More and more, through experience, I grasped the perversity of the said law, and when I began to put it into Latin I found so many fables, falsehoods and blasphemies, the same things repeated throughout in very many places, that I, wearied, gave it up. And in my distress over the said blasphemies I wrote some letters to the Church Triumphant, in the manner of a complaint of a bitter spirit. Now, however, my intention is, trusting in the highest truth, to refute the principal obscenities of the perfidious law.
licence_note: Public Domain Mark 1.0 per archive.org metadata (1608 print). English is the team's own literal translation.
keys: magis ac magis per experientiam apprehendi
tot inveni fabulas, falsitates, & blasphemias
Nunc autem est mea intentio
what_it_says: Riccoldo says he studied the Qur'an in Baghdad and learned Arabic, and found so many fables, falsehoods and blasphemies that he gave up translating it. He says he wrote letters of complaint and now means to refute its principal errors.
context: This is the author's own account at the start of the treatise, placing his study in Baghdad (Valdacum) and explaining why he wrote and how he organized the work into chapters. It is the best source for his method and his claim to have read the Qur'an in Arabic.
limits: Autobiographical claim, not checked against other sources except the Laurent 1864 editor's note that Riccoldo wrote in the East. The phrase 'Valdacum' (Baghdad) is the 1608 form; the 1550 Picenus version reads 'Babylona'. The 'letters' (Epistolae ad Ecclesiam triumphantem) were not read in this session; their title 'de perditione Acconis' is UNVERIFIED.

ref: Divina Commedia, Inferno, Canto XXVIII, vv. 28-33 (Maometto)
quote_orig: Mentre che tutto in lui veder m'attacco, / guardommi e con le man s'aperse il petto, / dicendo: "Or vedi com'io mi dilacco! / vedi come storpiato è Mäometto! / Dinanzi a me sen va piangendo Alì, / fesso nel volto dal mento al ciuffetto."
quote_en: While I was all absorbed in seeing him, / He looked at me, and opened with his hands / His bosom, saying: “See now how I rend me; / How mutilated, see, is Mahomet; / In front of me doth Ali weeping go, / Cleft in the face from forelock unto chin;”
licence_note: Italian text: Italian Wikisource transcription under CC BY-SA (page licence statement read); the Dante text is in the public domain. English: Longfellow's 1867 translation, text from Project Gutenberg eBook #1001 (release 1997; Gutenberg public-domain statement read). The 1867 date is UNVERIFIED in this session. Line breaks are shown as ' / '.
keys: vedi come storpiato è Mäometto
Dinanzi a me sen va piangendo Alì
Mentre che tutto in lui veder m'attacco
what_it_says: Dante shows Muhammad in Hell, his body split from chin to groin, speaking of his own mutilation; Ali walks ahead of him weeping with his face split from forehead to chin. Muhammad's punishment is for schism.
context: This is canto XXVIII of Inferno, in the ninth bolgia where schismatics are punished. Muhammad is the first sinner Dante meets there, and the passage is a literary image of punishment, not an argument about Islam.
limits: Literary, not doctrinal: Dante does not argue about the Qur'an. The Wikisource text spells 'Mäometto' with an umlaut; the team should check the spelling against a critical edition (the Petrocchi and Dartmouth editions were not checked: the Dartmouth page returned 404 through curl). Ali's presence is Dante's choice, not a historical claim.

ref: Divina Commedia, Inferno, Canto XXVIII, vv. 34-39 (the sinners of the ninth bolgia, including Muhammad)
quote_orig: E tutti li altri che tu vedi qui, / seminator di scandalo e di scisma / fuor vivi, e però son fessi così. / Un diavolo è qua dietro che n’accisma / sì crudelmente, al taglio de la spada / rimettendo ciascun di questa risma,
quote_en: And all the others whom thou here beholdest, / Disseminators of scandal and of schism / While living were, and therefore are cleft thus. / A devil is behind here, who doth cleave us / Thus cruelly, unto the falchion’s edge / Putting again each one of all this ream,
licence_note: Italian: Italian Wikisource transcription (CC BY-SA). English: Longfellow 1867 via Gutenberg eBook #1001 (1867 date UNVERIFIED in this session).
keys: seminator di scandalo e di scisma
fessi così
Un diavolo è qua dietro che n’accisma
what_it_says: Dante groups Muhammad with the other sowers of scandal and schism, whom a demon cleaves with a sword each time they complete the circuit of the ditch, and whose wounds close before they pass again.
context: The lines are the narrator's own classification of the sinners (seminatori di scandalo e di scisma), immediately after Muhammad's speech. They place Muhammad in the category of schism, which is the basis of Dante's view of him.
limits: Dante's category is 'schism' (a Christian ecclesiastical sin), which he applies to Muhammad as founder of a division from the Church; this is a poetic classification, not an argument. The sword in line 38 is the demon's instrument of punishment, not a call to kill.
